interactive.title: The mobile
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: This is a short lesson on a hanging mobile, in fourteen small screens. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it. The mobile has one or two levels. Each level is a straight bar hanging by a string from its pivot. Weights hang from the bars on strings, each marked with its weight in newtons. A box marked "?" is a mystery weight. Under each pivot sit two gauges, a clockwise one and an anticlockwise one. Each lists force × distance for every weight on its side. It shows the total in N cm. Each weight has a distance readout. It is measured from the pivot, never from the end of the bar. On screens 2, 4 and 6 a weight can be dragged along its bar, and on screen 10 the pivot. Positions snap to every half centimetre. A weight goes up to 40 cm from its pivot. Tapping a lower level folds it into one weight at its hook, marked with its total. Here is the rule the picture follows. A weight's moment about a pivot is its force × its distance from the pivot. That distance is measured at right angles to the force. Weights hang straight down, so on a level bar that is the distance along the bar. As you look at the screen, a weight on the left turns its bar anticlockwise. A weight on the right turns it clockwise. Moments on one side add. Each bar tilts towards the side with the bigger total. It hangs level when the two totals match. A string holds up everything below it. So the bar above feels a lower level as its total weight, at its hook. With distances in centimetres, moments come out in newton centimetres, N cm. The screens, in order. Screen 1, do, Which way will it tip?: one bar, held level by a peg, with 4 N hanging 30 cm left of the pivot and 6 N hanging 15 cm right. The gauges are hidden. "The peg is about to come out. Which way will the bar tip?" Choices, in a column: Left side down (right); Right side down; It stays level. Hint on Right side down: "The 6 N is heavier, but the 4 N hangs twice as far out." Hint on It stays level: "Level needs the turning effects on the two sides to match. Do they?" Read: "A 4 N weight hangs 30 cm left of the pivot and a 6 N weight 15 cm right. Which way will the bar tip?" Why: the 4 N turns the bar with 4 × 30 = 120 N cm. The 6 N turns it the other way with 6 × 15 = 90 N cm. The bigger turning effect wins. So the left side goes down, even though its weight is lighter. After Check the peg comes out and the bar tips left side down. Screen 2, show, Force times distance: the same bar with its gauges. Words: "A weight's turning effect is its force × its distance from the pivot. You know this as its moment. The 4 N at 30 cm makes 120 N cm anticlockwise. The 6 N at 15 cm makes only 90 N cm clockwise." Then "Drag the 4 N weight inwards." Read: "When the 4 N weight moves in to 22.5 cm, it makes 90 N cm. The two gauges match, and the bar hangs level." Screen 3, do, typed, Where it balances: one bar with 3 N hanging 20 cm right of the pivot and 5 N on the left, its distance readout showing "?". "A 3 N weight hangs 20 cm right of the pivot. How far left of the pivot must a 5 N weight hang to balance it?" A typed answer: 12 cm, a whole number. Slips: 33.3 cm, "That puts the heavier weight further out. The heavier one hangs nearer the pivot."; 20 cm, "Equal distances balance only equal weights." Hint: "Work out the clockwise moment first. Then divide it by the 5 N." Why: 3 × 20 = 60 N cm clockwise. The 5 N must make 60 N cm too. So it hangs 60 ÷ 5 = 12 cm out. The 5 N weight's distance shows "?" until the answer is checked. Then it slides to 12 cm and the bar hangs level. Screen 4, show, From the pivot: a metre rule marked from 0 to 100 cm, pivoted at its 50 cm mark, with one weight on it. Words: "Measure each distance from the pivot, at right angles to the weight's string. On a level bar, that is the distance along the bar. A rule's marks count from its end. So take away the pivot's mark." Then "Drag the weight along the rule." Read: "The pivot sits at the 50 cm mark. A weight at the 70 cm mark hangs 20 cm from it. Its distance readout shows 20 cm." Screen 5, do, typed, Read the rule: the metre rule pivoted at its 50 cm mark, with 3 N at its 10 cm mark and a 4 N weight on the right. "A metre rule is pivoted at its 50 cm mark. A 3 N weight hangs at its 10 cm mark. At which mark must a 4 N weight hang to balance it?" A typed answer: 80 cm, a whole number. Slips: 30 cm, "That is its distance from the pivot. Add the pivot's 50 cm to find the mark."; 57.5 cm, "You took the 10 cm mark as the distance. The 3 N hangs 40 cm from the pivot." Hint: "Find each distance from the pivot's mark first." Why: the 3 N hangs 50 − 10 = 40 cm from the pivot. So it makes 3 × 40 = 120 N cm. The 4 N must make 120 N cm too. So it hangs 120 ÷ 4 = 30 cm out, at the 50 + 30 = 80 cm mark. The rule is pivoted at its middle. So its own weight turns nothing. The 4 N weight's mark shows "?" until the answer is checked. Screen 6, show, Add each side: one bar with 2 N hanging 30 cm left of the pivot, and 3 N at 10 cm and 1.5 N at 20 cm on the right. Words: "With two weights on one side, add their moments. Clockwise, 3 × 10 + 1.5 × 20 = 60 N cm. Anticlockwise, 2 × 30 = 60 N cm. The totals match, so the bar hangs level. Yet the right carries 4.5 N and the left only 2 N." Then "Drag any weight." Read: the same words. Screen 7, do, typed, Three weights: one bar with 5 N hanging 24 cm left of the pivot, and 4 N at 15 cm and 3 N on the right, the 3 N's distance showing "?". "A 5 N weight hangs 24 cm left of the pivot. On the right, a 4 N weight hangs 15 cm out. How far out on the right must a 3 N weight hang to level the bar?" A typed answer: 20 cm, a whole number. Slips: 40 cm, "You left out the 4 N weight. Its moment counts on the clockwise side too."; 17.1 cm, "You hung both right-hand weights at one distance. Each weight's moment uses its own distance." Hint: "Write the anticlockwise total and the clockwise total separately. Then set them equal." Why: anticlockwise, 5 × 24 = 120 N cm. Clockwise, the 4 N makes 4 × 15 = 60 N cm. The 3 N must make up the other 60 N cm. So it hangs 60 ÷ 3 = 20 cm out. The 3 N weight's distance shows "?" until the answer is checked. Screen 8, show, Fold a level: a two-level mobile. A hook 20 cm left of the top pivot carries a lower bar on a string. On the lower bar, 2 N hangs 10 cm left of its string and 4 N hangs 5 cm right. A box marked "?" hangs 30 cm right of the top pivot, and the top bar is held by a peg. Under it sit the top pivot's anticlockwise gauge, holding 6 N × 20 cm whether the level is folded or not, and the lower pivot's two gauges. Words: "The string to a lower level holds up everything below it. So the bar above feels the whole level as one weight at its hook, its total. That is folding a level." Then "Tap the lower level." Read: "The lower bar balances, because 2 × 10 = 20 N cm and 4 × 5 = 20 N cm. Folded, it becomes one 6 N weight on the hook. The hook is 20 cm left of the top pivot. So the top bar feels 6 × 20 = 120 N cm from it, folded or not." Screen 9, do, typed, The mystery weight: the same mobile. "A lower bar hangs 20 cm left of the top pivot. On it, 2 N hangs 10 cm left of its string and 4 N hangs 5 cm right. A box hangs 30 cm right of the top pivot. How much must the box weigh to level the top bar?" A typed answer: 4 N, a whole number. Slips: 9 N, "That puts more weight further out. The far weight needs to be the lighter one."; 2.7 N, "Count everything below the hook. That means the 2 N as well as the 4 N."; 1.3 N, "Count everything below the hook. That means the 4 N as well as the 2 N." Hint: "Fold the lower level into one weight at its hook first." Why: the lower level weighs 2 + 4 = 6 N at its hook. So it makes 6 × 20 = 120 N cm anticlockwise. The box must make 120 N cm clockwise. So it weighs 120 ÷ 30 = 4 N. The box shows "?" until the answer is checked. Then the peg comes out and the mobile hangs level. Screen 10, show, A bar's own weight: a bar 60 cm long weighing 2 N, pivoted 20 cm from its left end, with 1 N hanging from its left end. The bar's own weight is drawn as an arrow at its middle. Words: "You know that a bar of even thickness has its weight acting at its middle. Pivot the bar there, and its weight passes through the pivot. Then it turns nothing. Pivot it anywhere else, and its weight has a moment." Then "Drag the pivot along the bar." Read: "This 60 cm bar weighs 2 N. Its pivot is 20 cm from its left end. Its weight acts 10 cm right of the pivot, making 20 N cm clockwise. The 1 N at its left end makes 20 N cm anticlockwise. So the bar hangs level." Screen 11, do, typed, The crane arm: a model crane's arm on a tower, a 20 kN load hanging from its front end, a box marked "?" on its back end, and the arm's own weight drawn at its middle. "A crane arm is 14 m long. It weighs 12 kN, acting at its middle. It pivots 4 m from its back end. A 20 kN load hangs from its front end, 10 m from the pivot. What counterweight at the back end holds the arm level?" A typed answer: 59 kN, a whole number. Slips: 50 kN, "You left out the arm's own weight. Its middle is 3 m in front of the pivot."; 41 kN, "The arm's middle is on the load's side of the pivot. So its moment adds to the load's." Hint: "Find how far the arm's middle is from the pivot first." Why: the arm's middle is 7 m from its back end. That puts it 3 m in front of the pivot. Clockwise, 20 × 10 + 12 × 3 = 200 + 36 = 236 kN m. The counterweight hangs 4 m out. So it must weigh 236 ÷ 4 = 59 kN. These are example figures, not a real crane's. The box shows "?" until the answer is checked. Screen 12, do, mixed, typed, Two unknowns: a two-level mobile. The lower bar hangs 15 cm left of the top pivot, with weight A hanging 10 cm left of its string and weight B 20 cm right. A 6 N weight hangs 15 cm right of the top pivot. The whole mobile hangs level. "A lower bar hangs 15 cm left of the top pivot. A hangs 10 cm left of its string and B 20 cm right. A 6 N weight hangs 15 cm right of the top pivot. The whole mobile hangs level. What does A weigh?" A typed answer: 4 N, a whole number. Slips: 2 N, "That is B. The heavier weight hangs nearer the string."; 3 N, "Equal shares balance only at equal distances."; 6 N, "That is the whole lower level. Split it between A and B." Hint: "The top bar tells you A + B. The lower bar tells you how A and B compare." Why: both distances on the top bar are 15 cm. So A + B = 6 N. On the lower bar, A × 10 = B × 20. So A is twice B. Twice B plus B is 6 N. So B = 2 N and A = 4 N. A and B show "?" until the answer is checked. Screen 13, do, mixed, typed, The see-saw: a see-saw with a 250 N child 2.4 m from its pivot and a 750 N adult on the other side, the adult's distance showing "?". "A 250 N child sits 2.4 m from a see-saw's pivot. How far from the pivot must a 750 N adult sit to balance?" A typed answer: 0.8 m, to one decimal place. Slips: 7.2 m, "That puts the heavier person further out. The heavier one sits nearer the pivot."; 2.4 m, "Equal distances balance only equal weights." Hint: "Work out the child's moment. Then divide it by the adult's weight." Why: 250 × 2.4 = 600 N m. The adult must make 600 N m too. So the adult sits 600 ÷ 750 = 0.8 m out. The adult's distance shows "?" until the answer is checked. Screen 14, do, mixed, Which way now?: one bar, held level by a peg, with 5 N hanging 12 cm left of the pivot, and 3 N at 18 cm and 1 N at 6 cm on the right. "The peg is about to come out. Which way will the bar go?" Choices, in a column: Left side down; Right side down; It stays level (right). Hint on Left side down: "The 5 N is the heaviest single weight. Still, total each side's moments." Hint on Right side down: "The right has two weights. Total each side's moments, not its weights." Read: "A 5 N weight hangs 12 cm left of the pivot. On the right, 3 N hangs 18 cm out and 1 N hangs 6 cm out. Which way will the bar go?" Why: anticlockwise, 5 × 12 = 60 N cm. Clockwise, 3 × 18 + 1 × 6 = 54 + 6 = 60 N cm. The totals match, so the bar stays level. After Check the peg comes out and the bar holds level.
interactive.ignores: The bars, strings and hooks weigh nothing unless a screen gives a bar its own weight, and the pivots turn without friction. Each bar's tilt is drawn in proportion to the difference between its two totals, up to a limit. So you can see which side wins and by how much. A real bar out of balance swings, then tips until something stops it or it settles at a slant. Readouts give each distance as if the bar were level. Tilting a straight bar shrinks every right-angle distance on it by the same share. So which side wins does not change. Every weight is a force in newtons, not a mass in kilograms.

explain.text:
A mobile hangs level when the turning effects on the two sides of every pivot match. A weight's turning effect is its force × its distance from the pivot. Its weight alone does not decide it. You have felt this with a spanner. The same push turns a tight nut more easily at the end of a long handle. So a light weight far out can beat a heavy one close in.

You know that product as the weight's moment.[^1] Its distance runs from the pivot to the weight's string. It is measured at right angles to the string.[^2] Weights hang straight down. So on a level bar, it is the distance along the bar from the pivot. It is not measured from the bar's end. Hang 4 N 30 cm left of a pivot and 6 N 15 cm right. The left weight turns the bar anticlockwise with 4 × 30 = 120 N cm. The unit is newton centimetres. The right one turns it clockwise with 6 × 15 = 90 N cm. The bigger moment wins. So the left side goes down, even though its weight is lighter. Slide the 4 N in to 22.5 cm, and its moment falls to 90 N cm. Now the two match, and the bar hangs level.

With more weights, the moments on each side add. A bar is balanced when the total clockwise moment about its pivot equals the total anticlockwise moment.[^3] You know this as the principle of moments. Write the two totals down separately. Then set them equal.

A lower level hangs by a string. That level is not falling. So its string must hold up everything below it. The bar above feels the whole lower level as one weight at its hook. So you can [[fold a level]] into one weight, its total. Each bar's own string pulls up through its pivot. It has no distance from the pivot, so it turns nothing. On a balanced bar, you may take moments about any point. Use the same point for every force.[^4] The pivot is the handy choice, because its string drops out. With every force known but one, the balance fixes that one. That is how you find a mystery weight. With [[two unknowns]], write one balance for each bar. Then solve the two together.

In this model, the bars and strings weigh nothing. A real bar of even thickness has its weight acting at its middle. That weight adds a moment unless the bar is pivoted there. **A bar hangs level when its total clockwise moment about the pivot equals its total anticlockwise moment.[^3]**

analogy.text: A Wheatstone bridge reads zero when the product of one pair of opposite arms equals the product of the other pair. A level bar is the same kind of balance. Force × distance on one side equals force × distance on the other. Know three of the four, and the balance gives you the fourth. A bridge gives an unknown resistance the same way. The Murray loop test for a cable fault rests on the same bridge.
analogy.breaks: A bridge balances one product against one other. A bar adds up as many moments as hang on each side. A lower level folds into one weight first. A real bar out of balance swings away from level. A bridge's detector shows a current instead, one way or the other. That current grows with the imbalance.

practice.text:
- For a real lift, the marked safe working load and the lift plan come first. These sums show why a load further out turns harder. They do not replace either.
- Sketch the bar, mark the pivot, and draw each force as an arrow where it acts.
- Measure each distance from the pivot, at right angles to its force. On a rule, take away the pivot's mark.
- Fold each lower level into one weight at its hook. That weight is the level's total.
- If a heavy bar is of even thickness, add its own weight at its middle.
- List the clockwise and anticlockwise moments separately. Total each list.
- Set the two totals equal and solve for the one unknown.
- Keep one unit for every force, all kN or all N. Keep one for every distance, all m or all cm.

**Rule of thumb:** twice the distance needs half the weight. A force through the pivot turns nothing.

**Worked example:** a pole of even thickness is pivoted at its middle. So its own weight turns nothing. A 30 N bag hangs 0.8 m left of the pivot. On the right, a 20 N bag hangs 0.5 m out. What weight 0.4 m out on the right levels it? Anticlockwise: 30 × 0.8 = 24 N m. Clockwise: 20 × 0.5 = 10 N m, plus the unknown's moment. The unknown must make up 24 − 10 = 14 N m. So the weight is 14 ÷ 0.4 = 35 N.

**Common mistakes**
- Judging by weight alone. The heavier side goes down only if its moment is bigger.
- Expecting balance at the middle. Two unequal weights balance at unequal distances. The heavier one sits nearer the pivot.
- Taking a mark on a rule as the distance. Measure from the pivot.
- Leaving out a heavy bar's own weight when it is not pivoted at its middle.
- Mixing kN with N, or cm with m, in one sum.

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the clockwise and anticlockwise gauges at a pivot growing and shrinking until they match, and the bar swinging level, when you drag a weight along its bar.

checks.label: The moment of a force is the force × its distance normal to the force: each gauge lists weight × distance from the pivot for every weight on its side, and totals them

If an object is balanced, the total clockwise moment about a pivot equals the total anticlockwise moment: every bar drawn hangs level only when its totals match, and otherwise tips towards the bigger one unless a peg holds it

The distance from the pivot is measured at right angles to the line of the force: each weight hangs straight down, so its distance runs along the level bar from the pivot, and on a rule it is its mark less the pivot's mark
Each typed answer and slip is worked from the lesson's figures: 12 cm (33.3, 20), 80 cm (30, 57.5), 20 cm (40, 17.1), 4 N (9, 2.7, 1.3), 59 kN (50, 41), 4 N (2, 3, 6) and 0.8 m (7.2, 2.4)
With each typed answer in place and the peg out, every bar hangs level: the answers balance the moments
The choices follow the totals: 120 against 90 N cm tips the left side down once the peg is out, and 60 against 60 N cm stays level
Before an answer nothing gives it away: the unknown reads "?", and every gauge total reads "?"; after it, each shows its figure
A lower level hangs by one string, so the bar above feels it as one weight at its hook: folded it is one 6 N weight, and the top bar feels 6 × 20 = 120 N cm from it, folded or not
A bar's own weight acts at its middle: pivoted there it turns nothing, and pivoted 20 cm from the left end of the 60 cm, 2 N bar it makes 20 N cm, balancing the 1 N at that end
Every demonstration is over within 5 s of its screen opening and nothing moves during the 0.35 s screen fade; every answer's motion is over within 2.5 s

applied.problem: A bridge's detector does not only show which way the current flows: the current it shows grows with the imbalance, so the stated contrast with a tipping bar is wrong as written.
